title: The Mock Trial Online Trainer
subtitle: The Mock Trial Online Trainer (MTOT) was a project I worked on for a long time, and it turned out very nice.

sections.heading: Learning
sections.content: From the MTOT, I learned a lot about app creation. I learned how to use API calls and manage API keys, because I implemented multiple tools including authentication with Google Firebase, data storage with MongoDB, and AI responses with Groq. I also had to host the website on Vercel, since it uses API calls and can't be deployed as a static site.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.content: I faced many challenges while creating this app, but I was able to persevere.

sections.heading: Reasons for the MTOT
sections.content: I wanted to make this app mainly to help my club. When I created the MTOT, I was a captain of the Punahou Mock Trial team, and I saw that our team had a lack of resources for improving their skills. I made the MTOT to help our team improve and win states, incorporating the key issues we were struggling with.

sections.heading: Submissions
sections.content: I submitted the MTOT to multiple competitions, including the Congressional App Challenge and the National STEM Festival. I originally designed it just to have fun, to learn, and to help my club, but I realized that with this very polished app, it would be a great opportunity to enter competitions.

title: Small Language Model
subtitle: The Small Language Model I created was a great opportunity to learn how transformers and modern AI works.

sections.heading: Check it out
sections.content: I created an API using a Hugging Face space, which allows anyone to test out my Tiny Language Model. You can also download the files or see additional details about the model on my Kaggle page. Hugging Face APIKaggle page

sections.heading: Learning
sections.content:
From building my SLM, I learned a lot about AI and language modeling. To begin, I learned how the model of a basic Transformer functions. I looked into how each part of a Transformer actually works so I could fully recreate one in code. I made the architecture for my Small Language Model a simple Transformer. This model was based off of an image by Mayank Pratap Singh, except I used RMS Normalization instead of Layer Normalization. I also did not include dropout or a final layer normalization in my architecture.



I use the same setup with three distinct chucks or 'blocks' to process the data. Essentially, this is all done to predict the next word. The input block translates a prompt into something a computer can understand, then the computer runs equations to determine which word should be next, then that word is translated back into English.

In more detail, the input block turns a prompt into a list containing many lists of numbers. Each inner list is called a token embedding, and it represents a word or part of a word. However, the machine cannot understand what order these words are in. To fix this, I used positional token embeddings. This means that I have another list containing many lists of numbers. For each item in this list, I add it to the corresponding item in the prompt list. This will give us the proper input to the next block.

The main part of the model is the Transformer block. For simplicity, I am not going to explain exactly how the Transformer block functions and what it does, but I will discuss what special changes I made to this section.
To ensure the numbers are not too extreme, you need to normalize them. The basic Transformer architecture uses LayerNorm, but I used RMSNorm, which is more efficient and requires less data. I also used GELU instead of ReLU for an activation function, which just controls how data is modified inside the Transformer. I chose GELU because it generally increases the model accuracy and does not cause problems with dying activation.

Finally, after the Transformer block, we are given a single list of numbers, which represents a word or part of a word. This word is translated back into English by checking which word in the model's vocabulary matches most closely to this word. It also is slightly random to ensure it does not always produce the same results.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.content:
When I began this project, I was hoping to make it entirely from scratch. I tried to create my own dataset, and train it on my own computer. However, I quickly realized that this would not be feasible, because of how much data is needed and how much time is spent during training. To fix the time issue, I switched to training my model on Kaggle, which provides free GPU usage. This did mean that I had to redesign the code to work on Kaggle, but it made training over twice as fast, which was incredibly impactful.

However, finding a good dataset was much more difficult. I needed to find a sufficiently large dataset that was also simple enough to teach a very small model. I eventually settled on the Tinystories dataset for the main training data, and the Google Answers to Google Questions dataset for fine-tuning. The Tinystories dataset was created specifically to test making highly specific smaller sized language models, and uses two million stories that are around 1,000 characters long. The Google Answers to Google Questions dataset contains short answers to a bunch of short questions. However, both of these datasets were not very clean. For whatever reason, I could not download a good copy of Tinystories, so I had to remove a bunch of artifacts and nonsense characters that seemed to appear from converting it between Latin and Unicode. I also had to clear away any excess symbols in order to keep the base vocabulary for my model as small as possible, so that it would be able to learn actual words instead of just small subwords.

sections.heading: Reasons for making the Tiny SLM
sections.content: I started this project because I was curious about how modern large language models work. I understand that the basic Transformer architecture is not exactly what is used anymore, however, I believed it would be a great starting place. I did lots of research and decided to build my own model to test my understanding. Although I knew it would not be easy, it was much more difficult than I imagined. I kept running into problems, and even the final version is barely usable to tell stories. Still, I think this was a great learning experience, because I understand much more clearly how a language model works. I still do not fully understand why a Transformer works, but I do know how each part contributes and how to make one.

sections.heading: Final Result
sections.content:
After spending months building this AI model, I finally had a version that mostly worked. However, I was still not quite done. I wanted to visualize the output, because that allows me to see exactly what it has learned. In order to do this, I used Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) to display the model's vocabulary in a graph. UMAP takes the 256 dimensions that represent a single token, and condenses them down into two or three. The point of UMAP is to see a general grouping of tokens and understand how the model 'thinks' about different words. Although some of these groupings may overlap, this is actually normal. The data has been reduced into so few dimensions that some of the information gets lost. Because of how UMAP works, I decided to create two graphs to show both the larger concepts my model understands and also the smaller ones.



Above are the two graphs showing the model's vocabulary.

The left graph was made to separate out the individual groups, and show exactly what the model has learned. There are five total groups, and I labeled a few of the groups that I could understand. For example, the green group was mostly made up of tokens that would end a word, such as 'ing' and 'ed'. But for other groups, like the blue group, it is unclear what is similar between the tokens. The blue group contained numbers and the characters for the end of a paragraph, but also complete words like 'animals ' and 'stories '.

The graph on the right shows more of the general structure of the vocabulary, with two large groups standing out. I believe these two groups represent the beginnings and endings of words. The groupings of capitals and connectors are also visible in this graph. This shows how strongly they stand out from the rest of the tokens, because they are visible in both the smaller structure and in the more general structure of tokens..

If you want to look at the graphs yourself, you can check them out below. I think the 3D graphs are very interesting, because they show similar structures to the 2d graphs, except they make more sense.
